title: How things balance and float
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 4 'How Things Work' (spinning, balance, floating and sinking, designing a boat), and goes further into levers and simple machines, centre of mass and pressure. No textbook needed.
summary: Why does a steel katori float while a small iron nail sinks? Why does a tall bottle topple, and how can a child lift a grown-up on a see-saw? Your child finds balance points, builds levers and ramps, and finds out that no machine gives free work. They see why a knife cuts and a camel does not sink in sand, measure the upward push of water, and design and improve a foil boat.
builds_on: Class 1: pushes and pulls, push backs, gravity pulls down. Class 2: forces change speed, direction and shape. Heavy things need bigger forces. Class 3: arrows with size and direction, balanced forces, newtons and forcemeters, mass and weight, friction and rolling. Next, in Class 5: full force diagrams with resultant forces, air and water resistance, streamlining, terminal speed and rockets. Gravity and magnets get their own rungs.
subconcepts: spinning about an axis, and why spinners wobble
stable and toppling: a low centre of mass and a wide base
colours on a fast spinner: the eye holds on to what it sees
levers: pivot, effort and load, and the see-saw rule
the ramp (inclined plane), the wedge and the screw
no free work: a machine makes the force smaller but the distance longer
pressure: the same force on a small area presses harder
float or sink depends on how heavy something is for its size, and its shape
upthrust: water pushes up on anything in it
Archimedes' rule: the upthrust equals the weight of water pushed aside
the water's skin (surface tension) can hold up light things
goals: By the end your child can explain why a spinner spins smoothly when its stick goes through the balance point, and find the balance point of an odd shape.
By the end your child can make a bottle harder to topple and explain why, using the centre of mass and the base.
By the end your child can find levers, wheels and axles, pulleys, ramps, wedges and screws at home, and explain that a machine trades a smaller force for a longer distance.
By the end your child can explain pressure with a knife, a drawing pin and a camel's foot.
By the end your child can show that floating depends on shape and on how heavy something is for its size, and measure upthrust with a forcemeter.
By the end your child can design, build, test and improve a boat, changing one thing at a time.
words: the line, real or imaginary, that something spins around
the balance point, where all of an object's weight seems to act
a bar that turns on a pivot to lift or move a load
the point a lever turns on (also called the fulcrum)
a lever, wheel and axle, pulley, ramp, wedge or screw: a tool that changes the size or direction of a force
how much a force is squeezed onto each bit of area
to stay at the top of a liquid
the upward push of water (or air) on anything in it
how heavy something is for its size
to plan how to make something before you make it

days.title: Spinning things
days.goal: Explore what spins well and what wobbles, and see colours blend on a spinner.

steps.title: Forces so far
steps.do: Start by remembering Class 3. Ask: 'What's friction? What's a newton? Draw a balanced force on a book on a table. Why is rolling easier than sliding?' Then spin a ₹5 coin on its edge on a smooth table. Ask: 'What happens just before it stops?' (It wobbles, rattles faster and falls.) 'Which force slows it?' (Friction with the table and the air.)

steps.title: What can spin?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child predicts, spins and records each object in a table with four columns: Object / I observe / I wonder / I think.

steps.title: Build card spinners
steps.do: Do Activity a1: four card spinners with the stick in different places, one of them coloured in two halves. Test them now and again on Day 2. Ask: 'Which spinner spun longest? What do good spinners have in common?' (Round, flat, and the stick right in the middle.)

steps.title: Where did the colours go?
steps.do: Spin the two-colour spinner (blue and yellow) fast. Ask: 'What colour do you see?' (A greenish blur.) Say: 'Your eye holds on to each picture for a tiny moment, about a tenth of a second. When the colours swap faster than that, your eye mixes them.' Say: 'A disc painted with all the colours of the rainbow looks pale grey-white when it spins fast, because white light is a mix of all the colours.' Ask: 'Why does a fan look like a see-through circle when it's on?'

need: bangle, pencil, stone, lattu, eraser, steel thali
thin card, a katori to trace, scissors, toothpicks, glue, crayons

days.title: Balance, and why things topple
days.goal: Find balance points, connect them to smooth spinning, and make things stable.

steps.title: Finger balance
steps.do: Balance a ruler on one finger. Ask: 'Where did your finger have to be?' (In the middle.) Now tape two coins to one end. 'Where now?' (Closer to the heavy end.)

steps.title: Find the balance point
steps.do: Do Experiment e2: find the balance point of a ruler with coins, and of an odd card shape by hanging it from a pin. Then push a toothpick through the odd shape's balance point and spin it: it spins smoothly, even though it isn't round. Say: 'A spinner spins well when its weight is spread evenly around the stick. Scientists call the balance point the centre of mass.'

steps.title: Topple test
steps.do: Do Experiment e7: tilt an empty bottle, a bottle with sand at the bottom and a bottle with a sand-filled cap taped on top, and see how far each tilts before it falls. Ask: 'Which was most stable? Why?' (Weight low down: the centre of mass stays over the base for longer.) Then your child stands on one foot, then with feet wide apart, while you give a gentle push on the shoulder. 'Which is harder to topple?'

steps.title: Tree pose, Jenga, lattus and loads
steps.do: Your child stands in tree pose (vrikshasana): one foot pressed against the other leg, hands together. Ask: 'Where must your body's weight be, to stay up?' (Right above the one standing foot.) 'What happens if you lean?' (The balance point moves outside the foot and you topple.) If you have Jenga or a stack of blocks, pull out blocks until it falls: 'Why did it fall then?' Then ask: 'Why does a lattu have a point at the bottom?' (Less friction, so it spins longer.) 'Why do trucks carry heavy loads at the bottom?' Read the 'women who carry loads' perspective and ask its question.

need: an odd card shape, a pin, thread and a key

days.title: Levers: lifting the heavy with the light
days.goal: Build a lever and find the see-saw rule.

steps.title: See-saw puzzle
steps.do: Ask: 'You sit on one end of a see-saw and a grown-up sits on the other. How could you lift the grown-up?' (They move closer to the middle, or you sit further out.) Draw it: a plank, a pivot in the middle, a load on one side and a push (effort) on the other.

steps.title: Ruler lever
steps.do: Do Experiment e8: balance a ruler on a pencil, put a stack of coins on one side and find how many coins balance it at different distances on the other side. Write a table. Then use a long ruler and a short ruler over the pencil to lift a heavy book, and ask: 'Which lever made it easier? Which end did you have to push down further?'

steps.title: Lever hunt
steps.do: Your child finds levers at home and says where the pivot, the effort and the load are: scissors (pivot at the screw), a bottle opener, a nutcracker or supari cutter (sarota), tongs, a spoon prising open a tin lid, a hand pump handle, a door on its hinges, their own forearm (pivot at the elbow). Ask: 'Why are scissors for cutting cardboard long-handled?'

steps.title: Could Archimedes move the Earth?
steps.do: Do the first challenge question. Read the quote 'Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.' Ask: 'Is he right in theory? What would the problem be?' Then read the hint and ask: 'If a long lever lets you lift something heavy, what do you have to give up?' (You have to push your end a much longer way.)

need: a 30 cm ruler, a long ruler or plank strip and a pencil

days.title: Wheels, pulleys, ramps, wedges and screws
days.goal: Meet the six simple machines and the rule that there is no free work.

steps.title: Simple machine hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a2: hunt for the six simple machines at home and on the street and fill in the table. Ask for each: 'Does it make the force smaller, change its direction, or both?'

steps.title: Ramp test
steps.do: Do Experiment e9: lift a loaded toy truck straight up with the forcemeter, then pull it up a ramp to the same height. Measure the force and the distance each way. Ask: 'Which needed less force? Which went further?' Then say: 'A machine never gives you something for nothing. It lets you use a smaller force, but you must push for a longer distance. Scientists say the work stays the same, or a bit more because of friction.'

steps.title: Al-Jazari's machines
steps.do: Talk about voice v3: an engineer who wrote a book of machines over 800 years ago. Ask the voice's question. Then ask: 'Who do you think built the stepwells of Gujarat and Rajasthan, and lifted water with pulleys and bullocks for centuries? Are their names in books?'

need: a toy truck, books as load, a board for a ramp, the forcemeter from Class 3, a measuring tape

days.title: Pressure: knives, pins and camels
days.goal: Find out why the same force can press gently or cut, and apply simple machines to new cases.

steps.title: Finger and pencil
steps.do: Your child presses the flat end of a pencil gently into their palm, then the pointed end with the same gentle push (carefully). Ask: 'Same push. Why did the point feel so much sharper?' (The push is squeezed onto a tiny area.)

steps.title: Pressure in dough
steps.do: Do Experiment e10: press the flat end and the point of a pencil, a coin flat and a coin on its edge, into a slab of dough with the same weight on top, and measure how deep each goes. Then your child stands on a thick cushion or a folded mattress, first flat-footed, then on tiptoe. Ask: 'When did your feet sink deeper?' (On tiptoe: the same weight is on a smaller area.)

steps.title: Camels, elephants, knives and pins
steps.do: Ask: 'Why does a camel have wide, padded feet?' (Its weight is spread over a big area so it doesn't sink into sand.) 'Why is a knife sharpened?' (A thin edge puts the push on a tiny area, so it cuts.) 'Why does a drawing pin have a wide head and a sharp point?' (Wide for your thumb, sharp for the board.) 'Why do tractors on muddy fields have wide tyres?' 'Why does it hurt to step on a small stone but not on a flat floor?'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet: machines and pressure
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2: levers, machines and pressure in new cases, with force diagrams. Ask your child to say the 'why' answers aloud before writing.

need: a slab of dough 3 cm thick
a thick cushion or a folded mattress

days.title: Float or sink?
days.goal: Hear the story, test what floats, and find it isn't just about weight.

steps.title: Story: Selvi's Coracle
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Why did the coracle not sink with the heavy grinding stone in it?' and 'Why did Selvi put the stone in the middle and tell the man to sit on the floor?' Accept any answers today. You will test them over the next three days.

steps.title: Push the ball down
steps.do: Push a plastic ball or empty bottle down into a bucket of water with your hand. Ask: 'What do you feel?' (The water pushes back up.) 'What happens when you let go?' (It shoots up.) Say: 'That upward push of water is called upthrust.' Then do a floating dance: your child is a stone and sinks slowly to the floor. Then a foil boat, arms spread wide, 'floating'. Then a fish rising and sinking with breath. Ask: 'In a pool, how do swimmers stay up without sinking?' (Air in their lungs helps them float. Kicking pushes water down, and the water pushes them up.)

steps.title: Float or sink test
steps.do: Do Experiment e3 with a bucket of water and 10 objects, including a big steel katori and a small iron nail. Record guesses and results. Ask: 'Find the heaviest thing that floats and the lightest thing that sinks.'

steps.title: The katori surprise
steps.do: Ask: 'The katori is heavier than the nail but floats. What's different about it?' Accept 'it's hollow', 'it's wide', 'it's got air inside'. Say: 'Whether something floats depends on how heavy it is for its size, which scientists call density, and on its shape. Tomorrow we measure the water's push.'

need: a plastic ball or empty bottle
10 objects including a steel katori and an iron nail

days.title: Water pushes up
days.goal: Measure upthrust and see how shape and salt change floating.

steps.title: Weigh it in water
steps.do: Do Experiment e4: hang a stone from the forcemeter, measure it in air, then in water. Ask: 'Did the stone get lighter?' (No, the water is helping hold it up.)

steps.title: Foil and clay shapes
steps.do: Do Experiment e5: the same foil sheet as a tight ball and as a boat. The same clay as a ball and as a thin bowl. Ask: 'Same stuff, same weight. Why does the bowl float?' (It pushes aside more water, so the upthrust is bigger.)

steps.title: The floating potato
steps.do: Do Experiment e6: a potato sinks in tap water but floats when you stir in lots of salt. Ask: 'Why is it easier to float in the sea than in a pool?'

steps.title: Galileo's ice debate
steps.do: Talk about voice v2: in 1611 Galileo argued with Lodovico delle Colombe about why ice floats. Then try the voice's test: lay a steel needle very gently on water on a small piece of tissue. The tissue sinks and the needle stays on top. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: A scientist in the kitchen sink
steps.do: Talk about voice v4, Agnes Pockels, who studied the water's skin with a tin tray and buttons at her kitchen sink. Drop a little washing-up liquid near the floating needle: it sinks. Ask: 'What did the soap do to the water's skin?' (It weakened it.) Then ask the voice's question.

need: a potato, a big glass, salt and a spoon
a steel needle and tissue paper

days.title: The great boat challenge
days.goal: Design, build, test and improve a boat that carries the most coins.

steps.title: Build and test
steps.do: Do the project. Say: 'You have one sheet of foil, 20 cm by 20 cm. Design a boat that carries the most ₹1 coins without sinking.' Your child draws a design first and predicts how many coins it will hold. Round 1: build, float, add coins one at a time, gently, spread out. Record the number when it sinks. Round 2: change ONE thing (taller sides, wider base, flatter bottom) and test again. Ask: 'Where did you put the coins? Why does spreading them help?' (Keeps the boat level, centre of mass in the middle.)

steps.title: Float or Sink? card game
steps.do: Play the Float or Sink? card game (g1). Each card names an object. Players predict, explain, and can test with the bucket.

steps.title: Archimedes and the weight of water
steps.do: Talk about voice v1. Ask: 'When you added coins, the boat sank lower. What was happening to the water it pushed aside?' (More water was pushed aside, so the upthrust grew, until the sides went under.) Then do the second challenge question: did the bathtub 'Eureka!' story really happen?

need: the printed Float or Sink? cards

days.title: Review and boat show
days.goal: Explain everything and show the best boat.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1: spinning, balance, levers, pressure and floating. Your child builds each force diagram and explains the 'why' answers aloud before writing.

steps.title: Challenge sheet
steps.do: Do two or three items from Worksheet ws3 together, including 'how does a steel ship float?' Leave the rest for another day.

steps.title: Boat show and teach it back
steps.do: Your child presents the best boat to the family: the design, the changes and the results. Then ask the check questions. Finish with: 'Show me how to make the clay float, and tell me why it works,' and 'Lift this heavy book with a ruler and a pencil, and tell me what you gave up.'

need: clay, a ruler and a pencil

pairs: a well rope over a wheel

worksheets.title: Machines and pressure in new places

sections.p: On a ruler lever, 4 coins sit 5 cm from the pivot. How many coins balance them 10 cm away on the other side?
A ruler lever: you push down on the left end, a book sits on the right end, the pencil pivot is in the middle. Show the three forces on the ruler.
sections.obj: a ruler lever on a pencil

sections.p: Why is a door handle put far from the hinges?
opts: a push far from the pivot turns the door more easily

sections.p: Which simple machine is it?
A machine can make a force smaller, but then you must move it a ____ distance.
A knife presses down on a carrot on a board. Show the push of the knife and the board's push.
sections.obj: a carrot being cut on a board

sections.p: Which presses hardest into soft mud?
Why does a drawing pin have a wide head and a sharp point?
The ramp needed a smaller force but a longer pull. Why can't a machine give you free work? What would happen if it could?

Meenakshi says a long lever gives you free strength. Her brother Arjun says it does not, because you pay with distance. Who is right? Use what you saw with the ruler lever to explain, then say what Meenakshi got right.
A ship sails from a river into the salty sea. What happens?
A stone hangs from a forcemeter, under water, not touching the bottom. Show all three forces.
A camel stands still on sand. Show the two forces on the camel.
Why does a tightrope walker carry a long pole?
opts: it lowers their centre of mass and slows any tipping

sections.p: A needle can rest on water but a nail cannot. What holds the needle up?

experiments.title: What can spin?
experiments.question: Which everyday things spin well, and what happens as they slow down?
steps: Draw a table: Object / I observe / I wonder / I think.
Guess if each object will spin well.
Spin each on the thali or a smooth floor.
Fill one row per object.
Add two objects of your own.
experiments.predict: Ask before each: 'Will it spin well?'
experiments.observe: How long each spins and how it moves as it slows.
experiments.why: Things that are round and evenly balanced around their middle spin smoothly. Friction with the surface and the air slowly takes away their spin, so they wobble and fall.

experiments.title: Find the balance point
experiments.question: Where is the balance point, and does it move when we add weight?
need: thread with a small weight (a key)
steps: Balance the ruler on your finger. Mark the point.
Tape 2 coins to one end. Find and mark the new point.
Make 3 small holes near the edges of the card shape.
Hang it from a pin through one hole, with the thread and key hanging from the same pin. Draw a line along the thread.
Do the same from another hole. Where the lines cross is the balance point.
Check: balance the shape on a pencil tip at that point.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When we add coins, will the balance point move towards or away from them?'
experiments.why: An object balances where its weight is equal on all sides: its centre of mass. Adding weight on one side moves that point towards the heavier side. A hanging shape always swings until its centre of mass is directly under the pin.

experiments.title: Float or sink test
experiments.question: Which things float, and is it only about weight?
need: 10 objects: steel katori, iron nail, ₹1 coin, wooden peg, apple, potato, candle, plastic lid, steel spoon, key
steps: Hold each object. Guess if it floats.
Put it gently on the water.
Record floats or sinks.
Sort the objects: floats and sinks.
Find the heaviest thing that floats and the lightest thing that sinks.
experiments.why: Whether something floats depends on how heavy it is for its size (density), and on its shape. A hollow katori pushes aside a lot of water for its weight, so the water's upward push is strong enough to hold it up. A nail is small and solid, so it can't push aside enough water.

experiments.title: Weigh it in water
experiments.question: Does a stone weigh less in water?
need: forcemeter or rubber band and ruler
steps: Hang the stone from the forcemeter in the air. Read the force.
Lower it into the water until it is fully under but not touching the bottom.
Read the force again.
Compare. The difference is the upthrust.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the reading be more, less or the same in water?'
experiments.why: The water pushes up on the stone (upthrust), so the forcemeter has less to hold up. The stone isn't lighter. It's being helped.

experiments.title: Foil and clay shapes
experiments.question: Can the same material float or sink depending on its shape?
steps: Scrunch a foil sheet into a tight ball. Put it in water.
Take another sheet the same size and make a boat. Put it in water.
Make a clay ball. Test it.
Reshape the same clay into a thin bowl. Test it.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Same foil, same clay. Will shape change anything?'
experiments.why: A boat shape pushes aside much more water than a tight ball of the same material, so the upthrust is bigger. When the upthrust is as big as the object's weight, it floats.

experiments.title: The floating potato
experiments.question: Can salt make a potato float?
steps: Put the potato in tap water. It sinks.
Take it out. Stir in 4 big spoons of salt until it dissolves.
Put the potato back. If it sinks, add more salt.
Keep going until it floats.
experiments.why: Salt makes water heavier for the same amount of water (denser), so it pushes up harder. That's why it's easier to float in the sea.

experiments.title: Topple test
experiments.question: What makes something hard to topple?
need: a protractor or a book to rest against
steps: Bottle A: empty. Bottle B: a cup of sand inside, at the bottom. Bottle C: empty, with a small bag of sand taped on top.
Stand each on the table and slowly tilt it with one finger until it falls.
Notice how far each one tilts before falling (rest it against a book to compare).
Try each bottle on its side and upright: which base is wider?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which bottle can lean furthest without falling?'
experiments.observe: How far each bottle tilts before it topples.
experiments.why: Something topples when its centre of mass moves outside its base. Weight low down (bottle B) keeps the centre of mass low, so it can tilt a long way and still have its centre over the base. Weight on top (bottle C) raises the centre of mass, so a small tilt tips it over. A wide base helps too. That's why buses carry luggage low and why you stand with feet apart on a moving train.

experiments.title: Ruler lever
experiments.question: How can a small push lift a big load?
need: a round pencil as the pivot
a longer ruler or a strip of wood
steps: Balance the ruler on the pencil at the 15 cm mark.
Stack 4 coins on the 10 cm mark (5 cm from the pivot).
On the other side, find how many coins balance them at 20 cm (5 cm away), then at 25 cm (10 cm away).
Write a table: coins, distance from pivot on each side.
Now put the heavy book on one end of the long ruler with the pencil close to the book. Push down the far end with one finger.
Move the pencil away from the book and try again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you need more or fewer coins further from the pivot?'
experiments.observe: The coins needed at each distance, and how hard it is to lift the book with the pivot in different places.
experiments.why: A lever turns on a pivot. A force far from the pivot has more turning effect than the same force close to it. 4 coins at 5 cm balance 2 coins at 10 cm: coins times distance match on each side. With the pivot near the book, a small push far away lifts it, but your end has to move much further down than the book moves up.

experiments.title: Ramp test
experiments.question: Does a ramp make lifting easier, and what does it cost?
need: a toy truck loaded with a book or packets
books to raise one end 20 cm
steps: Hook the forcemeter to the truck and lift it straight up 20 cm. Read the force and write the distance (20 cm).
Make a ramp from the board, its top end on books 20 cm high.
Pull the truck slowly up the ramp to the top. Read the force and measure the distance along the ramp.
Make the ramp longer and less steep (more books spread out, or a longer board) and try again.
Make a table: force, distance.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which way will need the smaller force? Which way will the truck travel further?'
experiments.observe: The force and the distance for each way of raising the truck.
experiments.why: The ramp lets you use a smaller force, but you pull the truck a longer way to reach the same height. Force times distance comes out about the same (a little more on the ramp, because of friction). Every simple machine works like this: it trades force for distance, or changes direction, but never gives free work. Scientists call this the conservation of energy.

experiments.title: Pressure in dough
experiments.question: Does the same force press deeper when it's on a smaller area?
need: a slab of dough about 3 cm thick
a small book as a weight
a thick cushion or a folded mattress
steps: Stand the pencil flat end down on the dough and rest the book on top for 10 seconds. Measure how deep it went.
Smooth the dough. Do the same with the pencil point down (an adult holds the book steady).
Press a coin flat into the dough with the book, then a coin on its edge.
Stand on the cushion flat-footed, then on tiptoe, and see when your feet sink deeper.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Same book, same push. Which will sink deepest?'
experiments.why: Pressure is how much force falls on each bit of area. The same push on a tiny point is squeezed into a small space, so it presses much harder and sinks in further. Spread over a big area, the same push presses gently. Knives, pins and needles use small areas. Camels, snowshoes and tractor tyres use big ones.
experiments.safety: An adult holds the book over the pencil point. Keep fingers away from the point.

activities.title: Four card spinners
steps: Trace and cut three circles and one square.
Find the centre by folding a paper copy twice.
Spinner 1: stick through the centre.
Spinner 2: stick 1.5 cm from the centre.
Spinner 3: square, stick through the centre.
Spinner 4: circle coloured half blue and half yellow, stick through the centre.
Spin each and compare.
activities.outcome: Four spinners showing that the stick must go through the centre, and a colour spinner that blends colours.

activities.title: Simple machine hunt
need: a table with six rows: lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw
steps: Read the six names and what each does: a lever turns on a pivot. A wheel and axle is a big wheel fixed to a thin rod. A pulley is a wheel with a rope that changes the direction of a pull. An inclined plane is a ramp. A wedge is two ramps back to back that split things. A screw is a ramp wrapped round a rod.

Hunt at home and from the window: scissors, a tap, a door knob, a rolling pin, a curtain rope, a well or flagpole, a ramp, stairs, a knife, an axe, a zip, a jar lid, a bottle cap, a pressure cooker lid.
Write at least two things in each row.
For each, say whether it makes the force smaller, changes its direction, or both.
activities.outcome: A table of at least twelve simple machines found at home, with what each one does to a force.

project.title: The great boat challenge
steps: Draw a boat design for a 20 cm foil square and predict how many ₹1 coins it will hold.
Build it and test: add coins one at a time, spread out.
Record the number when it sinks.
Change one thing: higher sides, wider base, flatter bottom.
Test again and record.
Try one more improvement.
Show the family your best design, your record sheet and why it worked.
project.outcome: A tested and improved boat, and a record of every change.

game.title: Float or Sink?
need: a bucket of water to check
rules: Cut out the cards and shuffle them face down.
Turn one over. Everyone says 'float' or 'sink' and gives a reason.
Test it if you can, or read the answer on the back.
Right with a good reason: 2 points. Right without a reason: 1 point.
Most points after all cards wins.

cards.back: can float on the water's skin

big: How does a ship made of thousands of tonnes of steel float?
If machines never give free work, why are they so useful?
A spinning lattu stays up on its point, but a still lattu falls over. Why might spinning help it stay up?
Who should get the credit for a machine: the person who wrote it down, or the many people who built and improved it?
Why can you float more easily in the sea than in a pool?

challenge.q: Archimedes is supposed to have said: 'Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.' Could he?
challenge.hint: The saying comes from writers centuries after him, such as Pappus of Alexandria. In theory a long enough lever could do it, but the lever would have to be unimaginably long, and Archimedes would have to push his end through an enormous distance to move the Earth a tiny bit. That's the rule of every machine: a smaller force, but a much longer push. Ask: what is the saying really telling us?

challenge.q: The story says Archimedes jumped into his bath, saw the water rise, and ran naked through the streets shouting 'Eureka!' Did that happen?
challenge.hint: The story was written by a Roman, Vitruvius, about 200 years after Archimedes died. Archimedes' own books don't mention it. Galileo later argued the bath method wouldn't even be accurate enough to catch a cheating goldsmith. What Archimedes certainly did was write the rule of floating in his book On Floating Bodies. Ask: why might a story survive longer than the real work?

challenge.q: 'Heavy things sink, light things float.' Is that true?
challenge.hint: A steel ship is heavy and floats. A grain of sand is light and sinks. What matters is how heavy something is for its size, and its shape.

perspectives.who: Women who carry loads on their heads
perspectives.view: Across India, women carry pots, bricks and bundles of firewood on their heads, often with a coiled cloth ring. A load kept right above the spine keeps the centre of mass over the feet. Ask: who taught them this, and why is their skill rarely called science?
Traditional fishing boats like the vallam are made of wood and shaped long and narrow. Ask: why might a narrow boat be faster but a wide one safer?

Over 4,000 years ago, Lothal may have had one of the oldest docks in the world, where boats came in with goods. Archaeologists still debate whether a big basin there was a dockyard or a water tank. Ask: what clues would tell you?

A camel walks on soft, hot sand all day, and narrow feet would sink in. Their wide, padded feet spread their weight over a big area, so the pressure is small and they sink in less. Ask: why is it harder to walk on soft sand in heeled shoes than barefoot?

A fish needs to stay at one depth without swimming all the time. Many fish have a gas bag inside them called a swim bladder. By adding or removing gas, they change how much water they push aside, so they can rise, sink or hover. Ask: how is a fish like a submarine?

perspectives.who: A swimmer floating in a pool
perspectives.view: Floating on your back, you feel almost weightless, yet the Earth pulls you exactly as hard as on land. The water's upthrust is holding you instead of the ground. Ask: if you can't feel gravity in a pool, how do you know it's still there?

voices.idea: In his book On Floating Bodies, Archimedes wrote that anything in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside. A floating object pushes aside its own weight of water. In other work he worked out the law of the lever: weights balance when weight times distance from the pivot are equal on both sides.
voices.then: His work was copied and studied for centuries by Greek, Arab and later European scholars.
voices.now: Accepted. Archimedes' principle is still used to design every ship and submarine, and his law of the lever is in every physics book.
voices.ask: Our stone seemed lighter in water and our boat sank lower with each coin. Can you use Archimedes' idea to explain both?

voices.who: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) and Lodovico delle Colombe, Italy (debate of 1611)
voices.idea: Delle Colombe and others said ice floats because of its flat shape. Galileo said ice floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water (ice takes up more space than the water it froze from).
voices.then: They argued in Florence. Delle Colombe showed that a thin chip of ebony wood floats but a ball of ebony sinks, to argue that shape decides. Galileo replied that the chip floated only because it sat dry on top of the water, not fully in it.
voices.now: Galileo was right about ice: it is less dense than water, whatever its shape. But delle Colombe's chip shows something real too: the surface of water can hold up very light, flat things (surface tension), the way a pond skater stands on water.
voices.ask: Our needle rested on the water's skin. Who does this help, Galileo or delle Colombe? Can two people in an argument both be partly right?

voices.who: Ismail al-Jazari (1136–1206), engineer at the Artuqid court in Diyarbakır (now in Turkey)
voices.idea: In 1206 al-Jazari finished The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, with drawings and instructions for about fifty machines: water-raising machines worked by animals and water wheels, clocks such as the famous elephant clock, and pumps and automata. He described how to build them so others could copy them. They include a boat of mechanical musicians whose drum rhythm could be changed by moving pegs on a turning drum, which some historians call an early programmable machine.
voices.then: The book was copied by hand for centuries in the Islamic world. For a long time European histories of engineering hardly mentioned it.
voices.now: Historians of technology now recognise him as one of the great engineers of the Middle Ages. They still debate which of his parts were truly first (for example his use of a crank and connecting rod in a pump) and which he improved from older engineers in Persia, India, Greece and China.
voices.ask: Al-Jazari wrote his machines down. The builders of India's stepwells and water lifts mostly didn't. Whose work do we remember, and why?

voices.idea: Pockels was not allowed to study at a university because she was a woman. Washing dishes at home, she noticed that greasy and soapy water behaved differently. She built a trough from a tin tray, used small buttons and a balance, and measured how films of oil and soap change the 'skin' of water (surface tension).
voices.then: In 1891 she wrote to Lord Rayleigh, a leading British physicist, describing her results. He was so impressed that he sent her letter to the journal Nature, which published it.
voices.now: Her method is the basis of the trough later improved by Irving Langmuir, who won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on surface films. Pockels received an honorary doctorate in 1932, when she was 70. She is now recognised as a founder of surface science.
voices.ask: Pockels did real science at a kitchen sink. What could you study at yours? Why do you think her name is so much less known than Langmuir's?

books.title: Who Sank the Boat?
books.author: Pamela Allen
books.why: A cow, a donkey, a sheep, a pig and a tiny mouse get into a boat. Who really sank it? Great for talking about balance and load.

books.title: Mr Archimedes' Bath
books.author: Pamela Allen
books.why: A funny take on why the bath overflows. Read it, then do the upthrust test.

books.title: Simple Machines
books.author: David A. Adler
books.why: A clear picture book on levers, wheels, ramps, wedges and screws.

books.title: The Way Things Work Now
books.author: David Macaulay
books.why: The pages on levers, pulleys, floating, ships and spinning wheels, with the famous woolly mammoth.

check.q: Why does a spinner with the stick at its centre spin better?
check.a: Its weight is spread evenly round the stick, so it doesn't wobble.

check.q: How can you make a bottle harder to topple?
check.a: Put weight low down and give it a wide base, so its centre of mass stays over the base.

check.q: On a lever, how can a small push lift a big load?
check.a: Push far from the pivot with the load close to it. Your end moves further than the load does.

check.q: What is the rule about machines and free work?
check.a: A machine can make the force smaller, but you must push for a longer distance. It never gives free work.

check.q: Why does a sharp knife cut, and why do camels have wide feet?
check.a: A thin edge puts the force on a tiny area, so the pressure is big. Wide feet spread the weight, so the pressure is small.

check.q: What is upthrust, and why does a steel katori float but a nail sink?
check.a: The upward push of water. The hollow katori pushes aside lots of water so the upthrust is big enough. The solid nail can't.

check.q: In the boat challenge, why did we change only one thing each time?
check.a: So we knew which change made the difference.

story.title: Selvi's Coracle
text: I am a coracle, a round boat on the Kaveri river at Hogenakkal. I am made of split bamboo, woven like a basket, and covered with a plastic sheet painted with tar, so no water gets in. I have no front and no back. Selvi rows me with one paddle. When she wants to make the visitors laugh, she spins me round and round.
Most mornings I carry people across the river to the rocks below the falls. The water roars there, and the spray hangs in the air like smoke.

One morning a man came down the steps carrying a sack, with his daughter, Nila, walking behind him. He put the sack down on the sand with a thud. Inside was an ammikkal, a grinding stone, as heavy as a small child.
"It's for my sister in the village across the river," he said. "Her old one cracked." He looked at me, and then at the stone. "This basket will sink," he said. "Stone sinks. Everyone knows that."

Selvi did not argue. She pushed me into the shallow water and pressed down on my rim with her hand. "Press here," she told Nila. Nila pressed. The water pushed back up against her hand, and when she let go, I bobbed up again.

"The river pushes up on anything that pushes it aside," Selvi said. "This coracle is wide, so it pushes aside a lot of water. The more you put in it, the lower it sits, and the harder the river pushes back."

She lifted the stone in and set it down in the very middle of my floor. I sank lower in the water, a finger's width, then a palm's width. Then I stopped sinking. I was holding the stone, and the river was holding me.
"Now you," Selvi said to the man. "Sit on the floor, opposite Nila. Not on the rim."
He sat on the rim anyway, because he did not want his good trousers to get wet. At once I tipped towards him, and cold river water slopped in over my edge.
"Down," said Selvi, and he slid down onto the floor. I came level again.

Selvi explained while she rowed. "When you sit high up on one side, your weight leans out over the water, and the coracle tips. When you sit low and near the middle, your weight stays over the middle of the boat."
Nila nodded. "Like the stone," she said. "You put the stone in the middle."

Halfway across, a gust of wind came down from the falls and turned me sideways. The man grabbed my rim and began to stand up. Selvi did not shout this time. She put her paddle deep into the water and pulled, and I spun. I spun slowly, all the way round, with the stone at my centre, and nothing in me slid or tipped. Nila laughed. Her father sat very still, with both hands flat on the floor.
"Why don't we tip when you spin?" Nila asked.
"Because the weight is in the middle," said Selvi. "The coracle turns round the stone, the way a lattu turns round its point."

On the far bank, the man's sister was waiting with her arms folded, as if she had expected the stone to arrive wet or not at all. Selvi and the man lifted it out together. As the stone left me, I rose in the water, a palm's width, then a finger's width, until I floated high and light again, the way I always do when I am empty.
The man paid for the ride back too. This time he sat down on the floor without being told, right in the middle, and folded his legs.
Before they climbed the steps, Nila crouched at the water's edge and pressed her hand down on my rim one more time, as if she was checking that the river was still pushing back. It was. It always is.
story.epiphany: A boat floats because the water pushes up on it (upthrust), and that push grows as the boat sinks lower and pushes more water aside. The coracle sinks only until the water pushed aside weighs as much as the boat and its load. The turn is the heavy stone placed in the centre and the man sitting low: weight low and in the middle keeps the boat from tipping, and lets it spin smoothly round its centre, like a spinner round its stick. Hogenakkal coracles on the Kaveri are real. Selvi, Nila and her father are made up.
ask: Why did the coracle not sink with the heavy stone in it?
Why did the coracle sink lower when the stone went in, and rise when it came out?
Why did the coracle tip when the man sat on the rim?
Why could Selvi spin the coracle without anything sliding or tipping?
What did Nila feel when she pressed down on the rim? What was pushing back?

ideas.idea: Water holds up anything that pushes enough of it aside.
ideas.more: Anything in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside (Archimedes). Hollow, wide shapes push aside more water, so huge steel ships float.

ideas.idea: No machine gives something for nothing.
ideas.more: A lever, a ramp or a pulley lets a small force do a big job, but you always pay with distance. This is one of the deepest rules in physics: energy is never made from nothing.

ideas.idea: Where a force lands matters as much as how big it is.
ideas.more: Far from a pivot, a force turns more. On a tiny area, a force presses harder. The same push can lift a grown-up, cut a carrot or let a camel cross a desert.

ideas.idea: Every object has a balance point.
ideas.more: All of an object's weight acts as if it were at one point. Put the support there, or spin it around that point, and it is steady. Let it move outside the base, and it topples.

unknowns: Who made the first boat, and how? The oldest boat ever found is a dugout canoe about 10,000 years old, but people reached Australia across the sea at least 50,000 years ago. So boats are much older than any we've found, and nobody knows what they were like.

We know why ice floats: when water freezes, its molecules lock into an open pattern that takes up more space. But water has dozens of other unusual behaviours, and scientists still argue about what causes some of them.

How did the builders of ancient temples and stepwells in India lift and place stones weighing many tonnes? Historians have good guesses (ramps, levers, rollers, ropes and huge teams), but for many buildings nobody knows exactly how it was done.
